words.text: A corner of the plan drawn again, larger, often at another scale on the same sheet.
A length the engineer wrote on the drawing, like 31'-8". Only a dimension can prove the scale.
The trade a sheet belongs to, the letter in its number: A architect, S structural, M mechanical, E electrical, P plumbing.
The designer who drew a trade's sheets and did its sums. The estimator prices what the engineer drew.
Part of the plan drawn again at a bigger scale, so the clearances can be read. Count what is on it once, never on both sheets.
A sheet of one trade's drawings, named by its letter: E electrical, M mechanical (HVAC), P plumbing.
The building seen from above, as if the roof were lifted off.
The written rules for the whole job, printed on the sheet: the pipe material, where the waste runs, and so on.
A short tag on the plan, a number or a few letters, that a column of notes spells out.
A thin line from a label to the thing it names. The app draws one, dashed, from a fixture or a diffuser to its run.
The key to a sheet's lines and symbols. The app draws its own on the sheet too: each counter and line type with its total.
The M-sheets: the drawings for the air trade, HVAC.
A diagram of how the power gets from the street to the panel, drawn as a single line.
The drawing's file, the form a set of drawings arrives in.
The drawing seen from above. It never shows a pipe or a duct going straight up or down.
The pipes drawn standing up, as if the wall were cut open. Some are drawn to scale, so the upright pipe can be measured.
How many feet of building one inch of paper stands for, like 1/8" = 1'-0". Every sheet has its own.
A printed ruler on the sheet. A shrunk PDF shrinks it too, so it cannot prove the scale.
A table on a sheet, one row per kind of thing. It is the engineer's answer key: the sizes, the loads, the air.
The building sliced through and seen from the side.
All the drawings for one job, the whole stack, one sheet per page.
One page of a set. Its number starts with its trade's letter: P-101, E-201, M-501.
A short label on the plan, like SD-1 or LP-1-1, that a schedule or a note spells out.
The box at the edge of a sheet with its name, its number and its scale.
A kind of work, such as plumbing, electrical or HVAC.
Drawn once, built everywhere the note says. TYP. OF 4 means four of everything in it.
A round of changes the designers send out before the bid is due.
A priced option the owner may buy on top of the base bid.
The main price, before any alternates.
The price a contractor offers to do the work. In the app, a bid is also one job you are pricing.
A trip back to a finished job to fix something, usually unpaid.
A priced change after the contract is signed. The owner pays it when the drawing was wrong; one you eat, you pay yourself.
Feet and tenths of a foot, rather than feet and inches. The app's totals are always in decimal feet.
What you send out: the report, the marked-up sheets, the paste into the bid.
Work with no engineer, where the contractor designs the system too.
The person who works out what a job will cost, from the drawings alone.
A line in the bid that says the price leaves something out.
A run's total feet.
The crew's lead on site, who builds from the marked-up set.
The company that runs the whole job. Your questions reach the designer through the GC.
Send the finished takeoff on to pricing.
The hours it takes to put an item in, from your own price book.
What a thing draws or has to handle: an appliance's gas, a circuit's power, the heat a cooling unit removes.
The course's own finished takeoff, its answer key. The whole-set chapter lays yours beside it.
A written question to the designer, sent through the GC.
A quick figure from the floor area, for design-build work. On an engineered set, the schedule's number wins.
Which work you are pricing, and what is left out of it.
The count and the feet together: the numbers the price is built on. A miss in the takeoff is money lost.
The power and light the builders run on during construction. It is never on a drawing.
The Americans with Disabilities Act. It sets the room a wheelchair needs and the reach range for switches and receptacles.
The heating and air engineers' society. Its standard 62.1 sets how much fresh air each room needs.
The model health code for restaurants. It wants a hand sink within reach of each food preparation area.
The International Building Code.
The International Energy Conservation Code: how a building saves power, such as lights that switch themselves off.
The International Fuel Gas Code: how gas pipe is sized and valved.
The International Mechanical Code, the rule book the air work must meet by law.
The International Plumbing Code.
Your town or county. It decides which code edition the work must meet.
The National Electrical Code, the code book electrical work is built to.
The National Fire Protection Association's standard for kitchen hoods and their grease ducts.
The sheet-metal trade's standards group. Its book of tables gives a duct's gauge and weight by size.
Underwriters Laboratories, the lab that tests safety equipment like fire dampers and lists what passes.
The free space a fixture or a panel needs around it, such as a wheelchair's turning circle.
Anything that burns.
The row of ranges, fryers and griddles where the cooks work.
A raised frame on the roof that a rooftop unit sits on.
The underside of the roof. The space between it and the ceiling holds the duct, the pipe and the wire.
The dishwashing room.
The canopy over the cook line that pulls out smoke and grease.
A place a duct or a pipe goes through a wall.
A stove.
A wall built to hold back a fire for a set time, such as one hour.
The concrete floor.
The built-in extinguisher in a hood. When it fires, the gas and the power under the hood shut off.
The clear space in front of a panel where an electrician stands to work on it.
A sink with three bowls: wash, rinse, sanitize.
Open air between the end of a drain pipe and the floor sink under it, so a backed-up sewer cannot reach the pipe.
A valve that sets how much water flows in a line, like the hot water return.
Black steel gas pipe, threaded together.
A smaller pipe or duct off a bigger one, out to a fixture or a diffuser.
British thermal unit. Gas load is in BTU per hour: how fast the appliances burn gas.
The main drain under the floor that the stacks empty into.
The pipe that takes all the building's waste out to the city sewer.
The frame a wall-hung toilet hangs on, one under every water closet.
A one-way valve.
A capped opening for clearing a drain. A grease duct has them too, to scrape the grease out.
Drainage fixture units: the code's number for how much a fixture drains.
Drain, waste and vent: pipe made for the drains.
In plumbing, anything that uses water: a sink, a toilet, a floor drain. A light fixture is a light.
The code's number for how much water a fixture draws (WSFU) or drains (DFU). The engineer sizes the pipe from the total.
A square drain set in the floor, that equipment drains into across an air gap.
The pipe that carries a gas water heater's exhaust out.
Feet per second, the speed of water in a pipe.
The kitchen's drains. They run to the grease interceptor, apart from the restrooms.
A sink kept only for washing hands.
A support, often a strap, that holds a pipe or a duct up. The code says how far apart they go.
An outdoor faucet for a hose.
A pipe that carries unused hot water back to the heater, so every faucet runs hot fast. Most bids miss it.
A drain that ends above a floor sink, across an air gap, instead of joining the pipe.
A tank outside where the kitchen's grease floats, cools and is pumped out.
Lavatories in a row on one branch.
A bathroom sink, a lav for short.
The big pipe or duct the branches come off: the city's water main, the gas main, the main duct from the unit.
What counts the water, the gas or the power a building uses.
The low sink a mop bucket is filled and emptied at.
The fixture-unit table's two columns: public (a restaurant, an office) and private (a house, a hotel room).
Plastic water pipe that bends.
Plastic pipe, polyvinyl chloride.
A pipe or duct that goes straight up or down. A plan is drawn from above, so it never shows one.
A valve assembly where the water service comes in. It stops water flowing back into the city's main.
The waste from toilets and sinks, and the pipe that carries it.
What brings a utility into the building: the water service from the meter, or the power's path from the street to the panel.
To suck water out through a pipe, the way a hose drains a bucket.
How far a drain falls per foot, like 1/8" per foot. Waste has only gravity to move it.
The plumber's cable for clearing a clog.
What comes in: the water pipes to a fixture, or the duct that carries air to the rooms.
The open top of a vent, above the roof. In electrical, the place a wire is fastened.
Screwed together, the way steel gas pipe is joined.
The U-bend under a drain that holds water, so sewer gas stays down.
The pipe from a fixture's trap to its vent. The code limits how long it can be.
A small line that drips water into a floor drain's trap so it never dries out.
A ditch dug for a pipe under the slab, priced by its length and its depth.
The main pipe or duct the branches come off.
In plumbing, the pipe that lets air into a drain, so the traps keep their water. In everyday talk, any opening air comes through.
The upright pipe that lets the drains breathe. It goes out through the roof.
A pipe or conduit that runs up or down a wall. The plan view never shows it, so the takeoff adds it.
Vent through roof: where a vent stack leaves the building.
The drain out of a fixture, the W on a schedule.
The trade's word for a toilet.
The tank that heats the building's hot water.
One wall that carries the pipes for the fixtures on both sides of it.
Water supply fixture units: the code's number for how much water a fixture draws.
The measure of current, how much electricity flows.
The current a wire can carry without overheating.
A circuit that runs from a panel out to its devices.
A switch in the panel that shuts a circuit off when it draws too much.
One breaker and the wires and devices it feeds.
A table of the circuits: each one's devices, its conduit and its wire.
A wire.
The metal pipe electrical wire runs in.
The unit plugs into a receptacle instead of being wired in.
A circuit that feeds one piece of equipment and nothing else.
Anything wired, such as an outlet or a switch.
A switch at a unit that cuts its power for service.
A pipe, conduit or duct that comes down to what it feeds. The Drop tool adds that upright length to a run.
The ordinary receptacle: two sockets in one.
Electrical metallic tubing: thin-wall steel conduit.
The ground wire that rides with a feeder, sized from its breaker.
The heavy wires from the main disconnect to a panel.
How much of a conduit's inside the wires take up.
Ground-fault circuit interrupter: a receptacle that cuts the power when current leaks through a person. GFI is the drawing's short word.
The green safety wire. The ground also ties the whole system to the earth.
The wire that ties the system to the earth, through the water pipe and metal rods driven into the ground.
Wired straight in, with no plug.
The conduit that carries a circuit's wires back to the panel. The plan shows it as a short arrow with a tag.
Wired so one starts or stops the other: the make-up air unit with the hood fan, the breaker with the hood's fire system.
A metal box where wires are joined.
A thousand VA.
The switch that shuts off the whole building.
The extra foot of conduit for the bend and the box. No drawing shows it.
The panel the service feeds first.
How high a device hangs on the wall. The app uses it for the vertical.
The wire the current returns on.
A switch that turns the lights off when nobody is in the room.
The metal cabinet of breakers that feeds the building's circuits.
One of the three live wires the power arrives on.
One breaker position in a panel. A two-pole breaker takes two.
A box the wire is pulled through. A run with too many bends between boxes needs one.
What the wire runs in, such as conduit.
A wall outlet.
The buried wires from the utility to the building.
A breaker that can be tripped from outside the panel, such as by the hood's fire system.
The clamp that holds conduit to the building.
The everyday building wire, named for its insulation.
Power on all three phases, for motors like a rooftop unit's.
The power company's equipment at the street.
The load a circuit is sized for.
The measure of electrical push. The building has 120 V and 208 V.
The voltage, the electrical push, a wire loses along its length, so the far end gets less.
The test after install that measures the air at every vent.
The total pounds of duct, the number a sheet-metal bid is built on.
Plain steel with no coating. A grease duct is welded black steel.
The most air a unit can move.
Cubic feet per minute: how much air moves.
The air a flame burns.
The wiring that starts and stops the units, and the thermostats.
A ceiling vent air comes out of.
The sheet-metal pipe air travels through.
The app's duct-sizing calculator.
A fitting that turns a pipe or a duct around a corner.
The straight duct on a path, plus a length for each fitting on the way.
The push a unit has to spare for its duct.
Air thrown outside, and the duct that carries it.
A fan that throws air outside, such as the hood's.
A shutter in a duct that closes in a fire, where the duct crosses a rated wall. Never in a grease duct.
A shaped piece that joins or turns pipe or duct: an elbow, a transition, a tap.
The soft, bendable round duct from a bigger duct to a diffuser.
Feet per minute, the speed of the air.
How fast the duct uses up the fan's push, per 100 feet.
A link that melts in a fire and lets a fire damper drop shut.
Steel coated in zinc, the usual duct metal.
A size by number, for wire and for sheet metal. The higher the number, the thinner.
The hood's exhaust duct: a chimney for a fire, of welded steel, with cleanouts.
A barred vent in the ceiling. Return and exhaust air go through one.
Heating, ventilation and air conditioning: the air trade, drawn on the M-sheets.
The measure of air pressure.
Sized to drop into one square of the ceiling grid.
Pounds per foot, the weight of a foot of duct.
Insulation that lines the inside of a duct.
A fire wrap a lab has tested and listed.
Outside air brought in to replace what the hood throws out. The MAU is the unit that brings it.
The round collar on top of a diffuser that the duct connects to.
More air going out of a room than coming in.
The fresh outside air a system brings in.
The space above the ceiling the return air comes back through.
A little more air coming in than going out, so the doors do not fight a vacuum.
A vent that can be shut.
Air on its way back to the unit, and the grille or duct it comes through.
A dashed box on the plan with a roof unit's name, air and power, and a leader to its hole in the roof.
A single box on the roof that heats, cools and blows the air.
The metal lost to seams and scrap, on its own line.
A steel collar that carries a fire damper through the wall.
The control on the wall that sets the temperature.
The push the fan has to give the air to get it through the duct.
A diffuser hung on no run. It counts toward no system.
A unit and the ducts and diffusers it serves. In the app, a group with an equipment tag.
Where a branch leaves a bigger duct.
Heated or cooled first.
A unit's cooling size.
A fitting that changes a duct from one size to another.
The speed of the air.
The fresh outside air the code requires for the people in a room.
A blade in the duct that sets how much air goes down a branch.
Insulation around the outside of a duct. A fire wrap is a listed one.
The layer you are working on. New marks land on it, and Clear Page clears only it.

Switched on and ready to mark. A counter is armed when the next click on the sheet uses it: one mark per click. Pressing M (Move) puts it down, and a number key or a click on the counter in the sidebar arms it again.
The counters, line types, quick keys and icons you keep for every job. They come to each new bid.
The app's checklist in the sidebar: what a bid must answer before it goes out. Some rows it judges itself, the rest you tick.
Count a fixture or a device and trace the run back to the last one, in one click.
The fourth verb: Bid Check says what the takeoff is missing or what does not add up.
An item that rides along on a counter or a line type: so many per mark, or one per so many feet of run.
A small label beside a field or under the cursor, like the size the Duct tool reads off the plan. The § chip, a section mark, names the rule behind a row.
Where a copy waits until you paste it.
The copy of your work kept online, in your account, once you sign in and save.
Arm a counter and click each thing it counts: one click, one mark.
A named kind of mark, such as WC-1 Water Closet. Armed, every click places one.
A box you draw that wipes everything inside it. Undo brings it back.
A file the app makes for you to send out, such as a report or a marked-up PDF.
The strip under the sheet that turns the pages, zooms and switches layers.

In the app, a gear icon opens settings: the one in the header opens Project Settings, and the small one beside a sidebar heading opens that section's. In electrical, the gear is the heavy equipment of the service.
A see-through copy of a typical, laid somewhere else to compare. It never counts.
Marks and runs the app totals together: a circuit on its panel, or a system on its unit.
The row of tools across the top of the app. On a drawing, a header is the beam over a door.
A see-through colour box dragged over part of a sheet, like a marker pen. It never counts.
A clear sheet laid over the plan, with its own marks. The sidebar totals count every layer; the Summary's by-page breakdown shows each layer's share.

words.term: The line beside Show me where
words.text: Every card ends with one line that says what the step is still waiting for, one thing at a time. It turns red when your last try missed and says why, and reads ✓ Done when the step is done. It is not the status bar at the bottom of the window, which shows the file, the save and the quick keys.
A named kind of run, by size and material, such as 1.5in Copper or 0.75in EMT. The app measures its feet.
One thing you placed on the sheet: a count, a run, a note.
The resting tool, on when no other is. It drags the sheet, and a mark in the wrong place.
A box whose counts are multiplied, for a typical drawn once and built many times.
Words you pin to a spot on the sheet. A note that starts with RFI: is a flag.
The keys 1 to 0 above the letters. Each can hold a counter as a quick key.

Your counters and line types, the lists under COUNTERS and LINE TYPES in the left sidebar. A returning device keeps its palette from bid to bid. A tool's palette is the small panel it opens, like the Drop sizes.
A run with corners, one click per corner.
A counter put on a number key, so pressing the number arms it.
The tool that boxes a room and reads its area and its air.
The app's list of the trade rules it applies, each one cited by its code section.
The path a pipe, a wire or a duct takes, traced on the sheet. The app adds up its feet.
A box with its own scale, for a detail drawn at another scale.
The column of lists down the left side of the screen. It holds the sheets under PAGES, your counters and line types, the SUMMARY and BID CHECK.
Holds each piece you draw level, upright or at 45°, however your hand wobbles.
The strip along the bottom of the window. It shows the file, the save and the quick keys.
The running totals, in the sidebar.
A small picture of a sheet, showing where every mark sits.
The pricing apps a finished takeoff is handed off to.
Click along a run, corner by corner. The app measures its feet.
A link that lets someone open the marked-up sheets and the totals, and look without changing anything.
A box on the sheet that changes the scale or multiplies what is inside it.
